title: What Is KYB? Know Your Business Verification Explained
summary: KYB (Know Your Business) is how US lenders, fintechs and platforms confirm a business is real, legitimate and in good standing, and find out who owns and controls it, before onboarding or lending. This guide covers KYB vs KYC, the US rules behind it, the 2026 FinCEN changes, a seven-step process and red flags.
body_markdown:
KYB, or Know Your Business, is the process of verifying that a business entity is real, legitimate, and properly registered. It also confirms who owns and controls the business before you onboard it or lend to it. In practice, KYB means checking registration, tax ID, and good standing, identifying beneficial owners, and screening the business and its owners against sanctions and watchlists.


For US lenders, fintechs, and embedded-finance platforms, KYB is the foundation of safe business onboarding and a core part of anti-money laundering (AML) compliance. This guide explains what KYB stands for, how it differs from KYC, which US rules drive it, and what changed in 2026. It also walks through a step-by-step KYB process, common red flags, manual versus automated KYB, and the questions compliance teams ask most often.


### Know What KYB Stands For Before You Build Around It


KYB stands for Know Your Business, and the industry also calls it corporate KYC or KYC for business, according to[Persona](https://withpersona.com/identity-glossary/know-your-business-kyb) and[Middesk](https://www.middesk.com/blog/know-your-business-kyb-identity-verification-explained) . Whatever the label, the goal is to confirm that a business customer is who it says it is and to understand the people behind it.


A KYB review answers three practical questions for a lender or platform. Does this business legally exist and operate where it claims to, and who ultimately owns or controls it? Does the business or anyone behind it present sanctions, fraud, or financial-crime risk that should change the decision?


For business lending, those answers matter before underwriting starts. A credit decision built on an entity that is not in good standing carries compliance risk and credit risk at the same time.


### Separate KYB From KYC to Avoid Verification Gaps


KYB verifies a business entity, while KYC (Know Your Customer) verifies an individual person. The two overlap because a KYB review includes identity checks on the individuals who own or control the business.


KYB (Know Your Business) KYC (Know Your Customer)


Who is verified A legal entity, such as a corporation or LLC An individual person


Core identifiers Legal name, EIN/TIN, Secretary of State registration Personal identity details and identity documents


Ownership review Identifies beneficial owners and a control person Not applicable to a single individual


Typical data Formation documents, licenses, industry codes, liens, judgments Identity documents and personal identity data


Screening The business and its owners against sanctions, watchlists, and adverse media The individual against sanctions, watchlists, and PEP lists


Common use cases Business lending, merchant onboarding, marketplace seller verification Individual account opening and consumer onboarding


The practical takeaway is that KYB contains KYC. When you onboard a business, you verify the entity and then run identity checks on each beneficial owner and the control person. A gap in either layer leaves the review incomplete.


### Understand Who Must Perform KYB in the United States


In the US, the formal beneficial ownership requirement applies to covered financial institutions under FinCEN's Customer Due Diligence Rule. According to[FinCEN](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/cdd-final-rule) , those covered institutions include:


- Banks
- Brokers or dealers in securities
- Mutual funds
- Futures commission merchants
- Introducing brokers in commodities


Fintechs and non-bank lenders are often outside that list, but[Middesk](https://www.middesk.com/blog/know-your-business-kyb-identity-verification-explained) notes that they frequently inherit KYB requirements through bank partners. If your lending program runs on a bank partnership, expect your partner bank to require KYB that meets its own CDD standards.


Online marketplaces carry a separate obligation under the INFORM Consumers Act. According to[Persona](https://withpersona.com/blog/what-is-kyb-why-does-it-matter-and-how-can-it-protect-your-business) , the law requires US online marketplaces to verify high-volume third-party sellers, and the EU's DAC7 sets a similar standard.


### Map the US Regulations That Shape Your KYB Program


US KYB requirements grew out of decades of anti-money laundering law. Knowing that lineage helps compliance teams explain why each check exists and which rule it satisfies.


#### Bank Secrecy Act and USA PATRIOT Act


The Bank Secrecy Act of 1970 established the foundation of US AML regulation, and the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001 expanded it, as[Middesk](https://www.middesk.com/blog/know-your-business-kyb-identity-verification-explained) outlines. These laws set the expectation that financial institutions know their customers, which is the basis for modern KYB.


#### FinCEN Customer Due Diligence Rule


FinCEN issued the Customer Due Diligence (CDD) Final Rule in 2016, with a compliance date in May 2018, according to[FinCEN](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/cdd-final-rule) . The rule is the most direct source of US KYB obligations for covered institutions.


Under the CDD Rule, covered financial institutions must identify and verify:


1. Any individual who owns 25% or more of a legal entity customer
2. One individual with significant control over the entity, known as the control person


A control person must always be identified, even when no individual meets the 25% ownership threshold. This matters for businesses with widely spread ownership, where nobody may qualify as a 25% owner.


#### INFORM Consumers Act


The INFORM Consumers Act applies KYB-style verification to online marketplaces rather than banks. Because marketplaces must verify high-volume third-party sellers, business verification becomes a requirement even for platforms that never extend credit.


### Track the 2026 Changes Without Weakening Your CDD Program


Two 2026 updates changed how beneficial ownership information is collected and reported in the US. Neither one removes a bank's or lender's obligation to perform customer due diligence on business customers.


#### FinCEN Exceptive Relief Under FIN-2026-R001


On February 13, 2026, FinCEN issued order FIN-2026-R001, granting covered financial institutions exceptive relief under the CDD Rule, according to[Troutman](https://www.troutman.com/insights/fincen-eases-beneficial-ownership-requirements-under-cdd-rule/) . Covered institutions no longer must re-identify and re-verify beneficial owners each time an existing legal entity customer opens a new account.


Instead, institutions can collect beneficial ownership information once and update it when risk or new information warrants a refresh. Institutions may still choose to verify at each account opening if their policies call for it.


Other CDD obligations remain in place, including written procedures, ongoing monitoring, and suspicious activity report (SAR) filing.[Troutman](https://www.troutman.com/insights/fincen-eases-beneficial-ownership-requirements-under-cdd-rule/) and[FinCEN](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/cdd-final-rule) both describe these continuing obligations.


#### Corporate Transparency Act Reporting Removed for US Companies


A FinCEN final rule took effect on August 14, 2026, according to the[US Department of the Treasury](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0603) . It permanently removed the Corporate Transparency Act requirement for US companies and US persons to report beneficial ownership information to FinCEN. Foreign reporting companies still must report.


This change affects what businesses file with the government, and it leaves untouched what banks and lenders must collect from their customers. The CDD Rule still requires covered institutions to verify beneficial owners and a control person, so lenders should keep their KYB ownership checks in place.


### Verify the Data Points That Prove a Business Is Legitimate


A thorough KYB check combines registration records, ownership data, screening results, and financial signals into one view of the business. According to[Middesk](https://www.middesk.com/blog/know-your-business-kyb-identity-verification-explained) and[Creditsafe](https://www.creditsafe.com/us/en/resources/blog/compliance/what-are-kyb-checks.html) , typical KYB data points fall into the groups below.


#### Business Identity and Registration


- Legal business name
- Registered address and operating address
- EIN or TIN
- Secretary of State registration and good standing
- Formation documents and business licenses


#### Industry and Ownership


- Industry codes such as NAICS, SIC, or MCC
- Identities of ultimate beneficial owners (UBOs)


#### Risk and Financial Health


- OFAC, sanctions, PEP, and watchlist screening results
- Adverse media coverage
- Liens, judgments, and bankruptcies
- Business credit and financial health indicators


#### Where the Data Comes From


KYB data generally comes from three places: the applicant, official records, and third-party screening sources. The applicant supplies information and documents, and Secretary of State filings confirm registration and good standing. Sanctions lists, watchlists, adverse media, and credit data then reveal risks the applicant may not disclose.


Cross-checking these sources against each other is what turns submitted documents into verified information. A mismatch between the application and official records is often the first sign that a file needs a closer look.


### Identify Ultimate Beneficial Owners to See Who Controls the Business


An ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) is an individual who ultimately owns or controls a business, even when that ownership runs through other companies. Under the US CDD Rule, the threshold is any individual owning 25% or more of the entity, plus one control person, according to[FinCEN](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/cdd-final-rule) .


Identifying UBOs matters because much of the risk in business onboarding sits with the people behind the entity. Once you identify each UBO and the control person, you run KYC on them and screen them against sanctions, PEP lists, and watchlists.


Layered ownership is where UBO identification gets harder. When a holding company or trust sits between the applicant and its real owners, your team needs to trace each layer until it reaches individuals. An ownership chain that never resolves to a clear UBO is itself a red flag.


### Run a Repeatable Seven-Step KYB Process


A consistent KYB process gives every business applicant the same level of review and makes your program easier to defend to partner banks. The seven steps below follow the typical sequence described by[Creditsafe](https://www.creditsafe.com/us/en/resources/blog/compliance/what-are-kyb-checks.html) .


1. **Collect business information.** Gather legal name, addresses, EIN or TIN, formation documents, licenses, and ownership details within the credit application.
2. **Verify registration.** Confirm Secretary of State registration and good standing, and check that the submitted name, address, and tax ID match official records.
3. **Identify UBOs.** Find every individual who owns 25% or more, name at least one control person, and verify each person through KYC.
4. **Screen sanctions and watchlists.** Check the business and its owners against OFAC sanctions, PEP lists, and watchlists, and review adverse media.
5. **Assess risk.** Combine registration results, ownership structure, screening hits, liens, judgments, bankruptcies, and financial health into a risk rating.
6. **Decide.** Approve, decline, or escalate the applicant, routing higher-risk businesses to enhanced due diligence before any onboarding or credit decision.
7. **Monitor continuously.** Watch for ownership changes, new screening hits, and lapses in good standing, and update beneficial ownership when risk warrants it.


Step 7 is where the 2026 FinCEN relief has the most practical effect. Because institutions can now refresh beneficial ownership based on risk, ongoing monitoring becomes the main trigger for re-verification.


### Escalate These KYB Red Flags Before You Onboard or Lend


Red flags do not automatically mean a business is fraudulent, but each one deserves a closer look before approval.[Creditsafe](https://www.creditsafe.com/us/en/resources/blog/compliance/what-are-kyb-checks.html) lists the following warning signs:


- A newly incorporated entity showing high volume
- Many businesses registered at a single address
- Opaque ownership with no clear UBO
- Directors linked to sanctioned entities
- Frequent changes in ownership or directors
- Registration data that is inconsistent across sources
- A history of insolvency


For lenders, several of these signals overlap with credit risk. A new entity requesting large financing, or a business whose registration conflicts with its application, should trigger both compliance and underwriting review.


### Compare Manual and Automated KYB to Scale Without Adding Headcount


Manual and automated KYB aim for the same outcome, but they differ in speed, consistency, and how well they handle growing volume. The right mix depends on your application volume, risk appetite, and partner bank requirements.


#### How Manual KYB Works


In a manual process, analysts collect documents, search state registries, and run screening tools one at a time. They record results in spreadsheets or case notes, which leaves room for judgment on complex ownership but slows onboarding as volume grows.


#### How Automated KYB Works


Automated KYB runs registration checks, data extraction, and screening inside the application workflow and sends only exceptions to human reviewers. That approach keeps clean applications moving, applies the same rules to every business, and creates a consistent audit trail.


#### Where Automation Fits Inside the Lending Workflow


Most teams land on a hybrid model in which automation handles collection, verification, and routing while analysts focus on escalations and enhanced due diligence. For business lenders, the biggest gains come from running KYB inside the credit application workflow rather than in a separate system.


That is where Lendflow fits for lenders and embedded-finance platforms.[Lendflow Automate](https://www.lendflow.com/lendflow-automate) uses its Doc Analyzer agent to extract structured data from PDFs, IDs, tax returns, and bank files. Its Industry Map agent classifies businesses by NAICS and SIC code, and workflow events such as missing documents trigger the next action automatically.


[Lendflow Connect](https://www.lendflow.com/lendflow-connect) adds a Borrower Platform for document upload, with configurable consent flows and stipulations.[Lendflow Intelligence](https://www.lendflow.com/lendflow-intelligence) then turns business data into lending decisions, with visibility into fraud indicators across the financing ecosystem.


### Apply KYB Best Practices That Hold Up to Partner Bank Review


Strong KYB programs share a few habits that keep onboarding fast without creating compliance gaps. Use these recommendations to tighten your process and avoid the pitfalls that commonly surface in partner bank reviews.


- **Collect KYB data at intake.** Request registration, tax ID, and ownership details within the credit application to avoid a second round of requests.
- **Always name a control person.** Identify a control person for every business, including those with no individual owning 25% or more.
- **Cross-check every source.** Compare the submitted name, address, and EIN against Secretary of State records, and escalate mismatches.
- **Screen owners as well as the entity.** Run sanctions, PEP, watchlist, and adverse media checks on each UBO and the control person.
- **Tier your review by risk.** Route higher-risk businesses, such as those tied to high-risk jurisdictions, to enhanced due diligence.
- **Refresh based on risk signals.** Use ongoing monitoring to decide when to re-verify beneficial ownership, in line with the 2026 FinCEN relief.
- **Keep CDD documentation current.** Maintain written procedures, monitoring records, and SAR processes, since the 2026 changes left them in place.
- **Align with your bank partner.** Confirm that your KYB standards match your partner bank's CDD program before launch.


The most common pitfall in 2026 is misreading the Corporate Transparency Act change. That change affects government filings only, so lenders that drop ownership checks on that basis risk falling short of the CDD Rule.


### Build KYB Into Your Lending Workflow at Intake


KYB, or Know Your Business, confirms that a business is real, legitimate, and in good standing, and identifies the people who own and control it. In the US, it rests on the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act, and FinCEN's CDD Rule, with the INFORM Consumers Act covering marketplaces.


The 2026 updates eased repeat verification and removed Corporate Transparency Act reporting for US companies, but bank and lender CDD obligations remain intact. KYB works best as a built-in step of your lending workflow, with automation handling routine checks and your team handling judgment calls.

### KYB FAQs


#### What Documents Are Required for KYB?


KYB typically requires formation documents, business licenses, an EIN or TIN, and proof of Secretary of State registration and good standing. Sources such as[Middesk](https://www.middesk.com/blog/know-your-business-kyb-identity-verification-explained) and[Creditsafe](https://www.creditsafe.com/us/en/resources/blog/compliance/what-are-kyb-checks.html) also list identity information for each 25% owner and the control person.


#### What Is Enhanced Due Diligence in KYB?


Enhanced due diligence (EDD) is a stricter review protocol for higher-risk businesses, such as those connected to high-risk jurisdictions, according to[Persona](https://withpersona.com/blog/what-is-kyb-why-does-it-matter-and-how-can-it-protect-your-business) . EDD usually involves deeper ownership tracing, more documentation, and closer ongoing monitoring than a standard KYB review.


#### What Is the Difference Between KYB and AML?


AML is the broader set of laws and programs against money laundering, including the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act, and the CDD Rule. KYB is one part of an AML program, focused on verifying business customers and their owners, while AML also covers monitoring and SAR filing.


#### Do the 2026 Changes Mean Lenders Can Skip Beneficial Ownership Checks?


No. The Corporate Transparency Act change ended FinCEN reporting for US companies but left the CDD Rule unchanged, according to the[US Department of the Treasury](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0603) . Covered financial institutions must still identify and verify beneficial owners and a control person for legal entity customers.


#### How Often Should KYB Be Refreshed?


Since FinCEN's February 13, 2026 exceptive relief, covered institutions can collect beneficial ownership once and update it when risk warrants, according to[Troutman](https://www.troutman.com/insights/fincen-eases-beneficial-ownership-requirements-under-cdd-rule/) . Ongoing monitoring still applies, so ownership changes, new screening hits, or a lapse in good standing should prompt a fresh review.
